title: Binary Search
description: Implement binary search on a sorted array. Compare recursive and iterative approaches, and understand the loop invariant.

data.text: Given a sorted array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, write a function to search `target` in `nums`. If `target` exists, return its index. Otherwise, return `-1`.
You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.

**Input:** `nums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12]`, `target = 9`

**Output:** `4`

**Explanation:** 9 exists in `nums` and its index is 4.
Maintain a search window `[left, right]`. At each step, compare the middle element to the target and narrow the window.

data.title: Iterative O(log n) — Standard

data.caption: Binary search halves the search window at each step by comparing the middle element to the target.
data.definition:
graph TB
    A[nums=[-1,0,3,5,9,12] target=9] --> B[left=0 right=5]
    B --> C[mid=2 nums[2]=3 < 9]
    C --> D[left=3 right=5]
    D --> E[mid=4 nums[4]=9 == target]
    E --> F[return 4]
    style F fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32

data.title: Loop invariant
data.text: At the start of each iteration, if `target` exists, it must be in `nums[left..right]`. When the loop ends (`left > right`), the window is empty and target doesn't exist.
Recursion naturally divides the search space. Each call searches either the left or right half.

data.title: Recursive O(log n) time and space
Recursive trade-off
data.text: Recursive approach uses O(log n) call stack space. The iterative approach is generally preferred because it avoids stack overhead and is easier to debug.
.NET provides `Array.BinarySearch` as a built-in method. This is the best choice for production code.

data.title: Built-in O(log n) — Production Ready
When to implement manually
data.text: Implement binary search manually when you need custom comparison logic, searching in rotated arrays, or finding boundaries (first/last occurrence). For simple existence checks, use the built-in.
